cells.tense: You are tending what is growing, and it is being tended without force.
cells.act: surrender the outcome and keep the act
cells.ask: Water something you're growing, then let the result be none of your business. No testing, no measuring, no better window. The act itself is the whole job.
cells.core:
You can let something grow without hovering over it. You give what's needed — water, time, attention — and then you step back, which is rarer than it sounds. What's under your care gets to develop at its own pace. You hold a fragile thing without squeezing it, and you don't need to see change to keep showing up.

What can bend is the scale itself. Fair measure, in a real week, is often what's left over once you stop adjusting. Next time you tend something, do the caring and then hand the result over — not the work, only the outcome. You water it because it's yours. What it does afterward is not your shift.
cells.sheetLine: You do the tending, then step back and let it be.
cells.verb: tending what needs room to grow
cells.place: in fair measure, keeping the scales level

cells.tense: You will keep adjusting the conditions so carefully that the thing itself can't be seen.
cells.act: sketch the whole of it badly, on one page, and keep the sketch
cells.ask: Get a sheet of paper and draw the situation you're managing, roughly, the mess and the parts you can't steer. Keep what you drew and change none of it.
cells.core:
When care runs hot, the effort outruns the thing being cared for. Every condition gets arranged, every risk gets handled early, and whoever or whatever is on the other side is held so carefully it can't move. Nothing wrong with caring; the scale has tipped toward managing.

Underneath is an outcome that hasn't been allowed to be uncertain yet. Draw it roughly — the worry, the shape, the parts that don't resolve — and keep what you drew. That page gets to be wrong. Let the next move come from what you actually see there, not from what you're bracing for.
cells.sheetLine: You'll arrange every condition before it can grow at its own pace.

cells.tense: Care was given here once, and the door it went through is already behind you.
cells.act: move toward the thing you actually want
cells.ask: There's something you want that has nothing to do with anyone else. Keep it to yourself and take one step toward it — small enough that no one benefits but you.
cells.core:
There's a held-back version of caretaking here — not much is being tended, and the independence is doing the work of a wall. What you want has gone quiet, and you've been calling that self-sufficiency. It isn't that you can't give care. It's that nothing is allowed to need you, and nothing of yours gets to need anything.

Don't try to push feeling back into that spot. Turn instead toward something you want, plainly, for yourself — one small step, no audience. The appetite for it is still in you. Steer by that and the caring returns by itself; it doesn't get willed back.

cells.tense: You are steadying others by habit and describing it as simply what you do.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Hand back one recurring task you carry for someone — the small one nobody asked you to take. Leave it where it lands, or let another person carry it.
cells.core:
People experience you as the one who steadies things, and your own account doesn't include the steadying. Somewhere along the way the caretaker part stopped being a choice and became what you are to them. You feel the weight and don't recognise it as work you're doing. The scale has been off-kilter in your direction for a while.

Set down one thing — not all of it, one small recurring handoff nobody officially gave you. Let it sit where it falls, or let someone else carry it. What's actually yours to tend gets clearer once one thing that was not yours to carry goes back into the room.
cells.sheetLine: They see the caretaker. You feel the depletion. Not the same person.
